title: Unconscious Competence or Why the Best Leaders and Performers Are Sometimes the Worst Teachers Leadership
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The article introduces the concept of Unconscious Competence -- the state in which mastery becomes so automatic that the expert can no longer trace the steps that produced it. As leaders and performers gain fluency through experience, the tacit knowledge underlying their success becomes invisible even to themselves, making self-reporting an unreliable guide to their actual practice. This is particularly pronounced in leadership, where excellence depends on intuitive pattern recognition -- reading rooms, sensing timing, judging situations -- rather than on codifiable procedures. The result is a paradox: the highest performers are often the least equipped to teach what they do, not because they lack expertise but because they have lost conscious access to the path they walked. Watching leaders in action and speaking to the people around them tends to yield far more insight than asking those leaders to describe their own methods. This helps explain why so many books by elite performers offer generic wisdom rather than transferable frameworks -- they genuinely cannot articulate the deeper machinery of their success.
points: * Unconscious competence is not a failure of reflection but the natural endpoint of genuine mastery -- when a skill becomes fully fluent, the practitioner stops consciously tracking the moves that produce it, which is precisely what makes performance automatic and fast. * Leadership is particularly susceptible to the articulation gap because its core competencies -- reading a room, judging timing, building trust -- depend on tacit pattern recognition rather than repeatable, verbalizable procedures. * The instinct to study great leaders by interviewing them is often counterproductive; observing them in context and interviewing the people who work with them typically surfaces far more useful insight than self-report ever will. * High performers' books and talks tend toward bromides not because they lack depth but because they cannot access the underlying mechanisms of their own excellence -- what they describe is what they consciously remember, not what actually drove results. * The implication for coaching is to move away from 'what do you do?' and toward structured observation and guided reflection, probing tacit knowledge through action rather than asking leaders to narrate their own expertise.
quotes: Top leaders and performers often can't fully explain how they create excellence because much of their skill is tacit, automatic, and built through experience rather than existing consciously." Page 1 "Once expertise becomes fluent, people stop noticing the steps, decisions, patterns, and cues that drive it, which is why experts often struggle to articulate their own know-how.

Leadership magnifies this effect because success often comes from intuitive judgment and reading people and situations, not just from repeatable procedures. This is why excellent leaders are not always the best teachers of their own excellence.

Over time, high performers forget what it was like not to know what they know now and the process it took to create mastery. So, the path that once felt obvious to them when they were mastering their craft becomes hard to explain to others.
Asking or interviewing them rarely reveals true insights. Observing them and speaking to those who work or compete with them typically exposes more insight.

Interviewing high performers, probing their tacit knowledge and action, especially by someone who understands unconscious competence, will often yield much more value than a presentation, book, or talk by them.

Perhaps this explains why so many of the books by elite performers, athletes, coaches, and leaders are simply full of bromides and obvious recommendations. It's not that they aren't expert. It's that they don't really know why." Page 2
